passage: You want the travel story? Fine, Pooja, it's Irfan and here's the awkward one. First week in the hostel town, I got a nice fruit seller to laugh by making the OK sign with my hand, thumb and finger in a ring. Big grin, big thumbs-up, the whole thing. His face closed up. A woman next to him looked away. Later a local roommate told me that in some places that ring sign is rude, and the thumb can be too. Then in another city, a shopkeeper beckoned me with a curled finger and I thought, is this a hello or a telling-off? I had no idea. Now I just smile, say "namaste" with a small nod, and watch what people around me do.

qa.q: What sign did Irfan make to the fruit seller?
qa.a: Irfan made the OK sign, with thumb and finger in a ring, along with a big thumbs-up.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the fruit seller's face closed up?
qa.a: Irfan was probably confused and embarrassed, since the friendly sign had clearly gone wrong. The face closing and the woman looking away suggest offence, though Irfan could not be sure at the time.

qa.q: What could a traveller do when unsure about a gesture?
qa.a: Smile, say a word or use a simple greeting like a small nod with folded hands, and watch what locals do before copying a sign.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller have seen Irfan's OK sign?
qa.a: The seller may have taken it as rude, even though Irfan meant it kindly, because the meaning of that ring differs from place to place.

grounding: A young adult travelling learns the OK-sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger carry different meanings abroad and falls back on a smile and a neutral greeting.

passage: I'm Pooja, and Irfan and I were on the coach to the coast when he tried to thank the driver with a thumbs-up and the ring sign together. The driver stared, then said something short in his own language and turned back to the road. Irfan went quiet. I couldn't tell if the driver was offended or only tired, and I didn't want to guess out loud. At the next stop a woman from the tour told us that beckoning with one finger is treated as rude where she grew up. Irfan tapped his phone, looked up how people greet there, and after that he used a small smile and a nod. The driver nodded back at the end of the trip. Maybe that meant it was fine.

qa.q: Where were Irfan and Pooja travelling?
qa.a: They were on a coach to the coast.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when the driver turned back to the road?
qa.a: Irfan was probably embarrassed and unsure, which fits the sudden quiet. Pooja notes the driver might only have been tired, so the reaction is not proof of offence.

qa.q: What small step helped Irfan afterwards?
qa.a: Irfan looked up how people greet there and switched to a small smile and nod, a neutral gesture unlikely to offend.

qa.q: Why might the driver react differently from someone back home?
qa.a: In some countries the thumbs-up, ring sign or one-finger beckon can be rude, so the driver may have read them very differently from how Irfan meant them.

grounding: An observer watches a young traveller's gestures misfire across cultures and sees a smile and a nod work as a neutral greeting.
